Magnetically responsive anisotropy

To validate the key steps in the design of the magnetically responsive anisotropy module, we carried out expression, purification, and fluorescence-based binding experiments for a magnetic-nanoparticle-binding protein. We first obtained a recombinant fusion protein containing the Fe3O4-binding peptide TVNFKLY and completed its expression, purification, and desalting. We then examined its binding to magnetic nanoparticles through FITC fluorescence labeling, co-incubation with the particles, magnetic separation, and washing, thereby providing an experimental basis for subsequently introducing magnetic-field-induced orientation into a SELP hydrogel.

4.1 Design of the Magnetic-Nanoparticle-Binding Protein

Experiment

The Fe3O4-binding capability of TVNFKLY has previously been validated through phage-display screening and multiple characterization methods [1]. We used TVNFKLY as the functional peptide in the experimental group and included GTWSLLL, which was expected not to bind magnetic nanoparticles, as a control to evaluate the contribution of the TVNFKLY sequence to particle binding. The experimental construct contained a His tag, a SUMO tag, a DogTag sequence, and the TVNFKLY peptide. The His tag was used for subsequent affinity purification, the SUMO tag helped improve soluble expression and stability of the heterologous protein [2], and DogTag provided an interface for subsequent connection to other protein modules [3,4].

Because this plasmid differs from the corresponding SUMO-DogTag plasmid by only 81 bp, we used a site-directed mutagenesis system for construction. The SUMO-DogTag plasmid was used as the backbone, and the TVNFKLY-coding sequence was introduced by high-fidelity PCR. The methylated parental template was then digested with DpnI, and Exnase II-mediated homologous recombination was used to recircularize the linear amplification product. The recombinant product was transformed into Trelief 5alpha competent cells, and single colonies were picked after selection on kanamycin-containing medium. Candidate clones were screened by colony PCR, and positive clones were further subjected to plasmid extraction and Sanger sequencing.

Results

We constructed an expression plasmid encoding 6xHis-SUMO-DogTag-TVNFKLY (Figure 4.1.1).

Single colonies suitable for subsequent screening were obtained on the transformation plates. In the colony PCR assay, multiple candidate clones exhibited the target band indicated in the original experimental records.

Agarose gel electrophoresis of the colony PCR products revealed a band at approximately 5,683 bp, consistent with the theoretical value (Figure 4.1.2). Sequencing results matched the designed sequence; therefore, the construct was advanced to expression validation.

4.2 Expression, Purification, and Concentration of the Fusion Protein

Experiment

The sequence-confirmed pET28a-SUMO-DogTag-TVNFKLY plasmid was transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) competent cells, and expression strains were selected on kanamycin-containing medium. A single colony was picked for small-scale culture, and IPTG was added under different induction conditions to induce fusion-protein expression. After induction, the cells were collected and lysed, and Western blotting was used to compare changes in the protein bands before and after induction or under different induction conditions. Based on the small-scale expression-screening results, the condition showing a more prominent band in the target molecular-weight region was selected for subsequent scale-up culture. In this stage, 1 mM IPTG was ultimately used to induce expression of the fusion protein.

Results

Western blot results showed that, after IPTG addition, an enhanced band appeared in the molecular-weight region corresponding to the target fusion protein, indicating that pET28a-SUMO-DogTag-TVNFKLY could be expressed in BL21(DE3). Based on the literature and preliminary screening results, the band in the target region was relatively clear under the 1 mM IPTG condition, and this condition was therefore selected for scale-up expression [5].

Experiment

After scale-up culture, the cells were collected, resuspended, and disrupted by sonication to obtain the lysate. The N-terminal 6xHis tag of the fusion protein was used for Ni-affinity chromatography. The lysate, flow-through, wash, and elution fractions were collected sequentially, and enrichment of the target protein was evaluated by SDS-PAGE.

Results

SDS-PAGE showed a relatively distinct enriched band in the approximately 25-35 kDa region of the elution fraction, whereas some contaminating proteins were mainly present in the lysate, flow-through, or wash fractions. These results indicated that Ni-affinity chromatography enriched the His-tagged SUMO-DogTag-TVN fusion protein.

Experiment

The purified elution fraction was further dialyzed or desalted to reduce the effects of imidazole, salt ions, and other small molecules on FITC labeling and subsequent particle-binding experiments. The desalted protein was concentrated using an ultrafiltration device. Samples before concentration, the retentate after concentration, and the filtrate were retained, and their protein concentrations were measured using the BCA assay.

Results

The BCA results showed that the calculated protein concentration increased from approximately 0.37 mg/mL before concentration to approximately 5.04 mg/mL after concentration, indicating that ultrafiltration markedly increased the protein concentration in the retentate. A protein signal of approximately 0.34 mg/mL was still detected in the filtrate, suggesting that small-molecule interference, membrane permeation loss, or measurement background may have been present during the concentration process.

4.3 Ligation Reaction

Experiment

To verify whether the purified SUMO-DogTag-TVN fusion protein retained DogTag-mediated conjugation activity, we used GFP-SnoopTag2 as a visual reporter protein and SnoopLigase2 to catalyze covalent ligation between DogTag and SnoopTag2. The reaction systems contained either SUMO-DogTag-TVN or SUMO-DogTag lacking TVNFKLY. A negative control lacking SnoopLigase2 was also included to exclude higher-molecular-weight bands caused by protein mixing or nonspecific aggregation. Each group was reacted at room temperature for 15 min or 6 h. After the reaction, SDS-PAGE loading buffer was added to terminate the reaction, and SDS-PAGE was used to compare the migration patterns of the substrate bands and the ligation-product bands.

Results

In the control group without SnoopLigase2, GFP-SnoopTag2 and SUMO-DogTag-TVN primarily retained their respective substrate bands, and no obvious higher-molecular-weight ligation product was observed. After SnoopLigase2 was added, a new higher-molecular-weight band appeared above the substrate bands. Its migration position was consistent with the expected molecular weight of the ligation product formed by GFP-SnoopTag2 and the DogTag-containing protein.

SUMO-DogTag-TVN and SUMO-DogTag both showed the same type of enzyme-dependent band change, indicating that introduction of the TVNFKLY peptide did not substantially disrupt the ligation function of DogTag. A ligation product could already be observed after 15 min, and the corresponding band remained detectable after extending the reaction to 6 h.

Therefore, these results support the conclusion that the purified SUMO-DogTag-TVN retained detectable SnoopLigase2-dependent conjugation activity.

4.4 Functional Validation

4.4.1 FITC Fluorescence Labeling
Experiment

To track the distribution of the fusion protein during magnetic-nanoparticle incubation, magnetic separation, and washing, we fluorescently labeled the purified protein with fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC).

The protein was placed in a carbonate buffer suitable for the reaction between FITC and protein amino groups. FITC was slowly added under light-protected conditions, and the labeling reaction was allowed to proceed. After the reaction, glycine was added to terminate the remaining FITC-labeling reaction, and unreacted free dye was removed using a desalting column [6]. The control protein was subjected to the same labeling and post-treatment procedures.

Small amounts of FITC-labeled protein and unlabeled protein were analyzed by SDS-PAGE. The nonfluorescent half of the gel was immersed in Coomassie Brilliant Blue G250 rapid staining solution, while the side containing the FITC-labeled protein was kept protected from light and was not stained. Images were acquired using the 532 nm and 302 nm imaging channels. One portion was used to observe protein migration and loading, and the other was used to compare the fluorescence signals of the labeled and unlabeled samples.

Results

Gel imaging showed a clear fluorescence signal in the FITC-labeled protein lane, whereas the unlabeled protein lane displayed only weak background. The fluorescence signal largely corresponded to the protein-band region, supporting the conclusion that FITC was associated with the protein sample rather than that the signal was produced entirely by free dye in the gel.

These results indicate that the labeled fusion protein had a fluorescence signal suitable for subsequent microscopic observation. However, because the dye-to-protein molar ratio was not measured and standardized exposure and band-density analysis were not performed, the present results only confirm successful labeling and cannot be used to calculate FITC labeling efficiency or directly compare labeling levels among different protein samples.

4.4.2 Magnetic-Nanoparticle Binding and Washing
Experiment

To preliminarily evaluate the binding of SUMO-DogTag-TVN to magnetic nanoparticles and its retention after washing, the FITC-labeled fusion protein was co-incubated with Fe3O4 magnetic nanoparticles. The experimental group used the fusion protein containing TVNFKLY, whereas the control group used the control protein containing GTWSLLL. Protein input, particle amount, incubation time, and buffer system were kept as consistent as possible.

A magnetic separator was used to collect the magnetic nanoparticles and remove the original dispersion medium. The labeled-protein reaction mixture was then added and thoroughly resuspended. Co-incubation was performed at room temperature in the dark, with periodic gentle mixing to ensure sufficient contact between the protein and the particles.

After incubation, the magnetic nanoparticles were collected using the magnetic rack and the supernatant was removed. The particles were then washed multiple times with buffer to reduce the retention of unbound protein and free fluorescent material. After washing, the particles were gently resuspended, and bright-field and green-fluorescence images were acquired to determine whether the fluorescence signal remained associated with the particle fraction.

Results

After magnetic separation and multiple washes, green fluorescence could still be observed in particles or particle-aggregation regions in some microscopic fields, indicating that FITC-labeled material could be retained with the magnetic-particle fraction in this experimental workflow. Under the action of the magnetic field, the magnetic nanoparticles changed from a disordered state to an ordered arrangement, and the green fluorescence aligned accordingly. This result provided qualitative evidence for magnetic-field-guided changes in SELP orientation [7].

GAG Retention Module

Overview

To validate the molecular basis of our GAG-retention module, we established a complete experimental workflow spanning plasmid construction, recombinant protein preparation, tag removal, and functional validation. The overall strategy was to first obtain a purified recombinant protein that could be used in subsequent experiments while retaining the CPC functional module, and then directly evaluate whether the protein could interact with glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), particularly chondroitin sulfate A (CS-A).

Therefore, we constructed the His-SUMO-AviTag-TEVsite-linker-DogTag-CPC expression system and used Escherichia coli for recombinant protein production. Following expression and purification of the fusion protein by His-tag affinity chromatography, ultrafiltration was used to concentrate the protein and exchange the buffer. The SUMO domain was subsequently removed from the fusion protein using ULP1, followed by reverse purification using the His tag and another round of ultrafiltration to obtain a CPC-containing protein preparation suitable for subsequent functional validation.

The processed protein was then evaluated for GAG interaction from two complementary perspectives. First, changes in CS-A electrophoretic mobility were analyzed to qualitatively or semi-quantitatively evaluate protein–GAG interaction. Subsequently, the retained AviTag was used for BirA-mediated enzymatic biotinylation, allowing the protein to be immobilized on streptavidin magnetic beads, followed by DMMB-based analysis of its ability to capture soluble CS-A. In this way, we could first validate the molecular function of the protein-level functional module before introducing it into the final SELP hydrogel.

1. Preparation of CPC Recombinant Proteins

To support subsequent validation of ligation activity and glycosaminoglycan (GAG) capture, we first prepared recombinant proteins containing the cationic peptide carrier (CPC). This section describes the design of the expression plasmids, establishment and optimization of the CPC recombinant-protein expression system, His-tag affinity purification and concentration, and SUMO-tag removal followed by reverse purification.

Experiment

Plasmid Construction and Recombinant Protein Production

The GAG-retention module required a recombinant protein that could be stably expressed while remaining compatible with downstream functional validation. Therefore, we adopted a modular fusion protein design: the His tag was used for protein purification, SUMO was used to facilitate recombinant protein expression and processing, the AviTag was used for subsequent BirA-mediated enzymatic biotinylation, the DogTag-containing region was used for modular conjugation, and the CPC sequence served as the core GAG-interacting domain.

After plasmid construction, the recombinant expression plasmid was confirmed and the correct construct was introduced into E. coli BL21(DE3). Expression samples were then analyzed to evaluate the production of the target fusion protein and its solubility distribution, and the established expression conditions were used for subsequent large-scale protein preparation.

The obtained His-SUMO-AviTag-TEVsite-linker-DogTag-CPC fusion protein was further purified by His-tag affinity chromatography. By comparing the distribution of the target protein among different purification fractions, we confirmed the recovery of the recombinant protein and obtained the target protein fractions for subsequent processing. This established the upstream experimental workflow from plasmid construction →recombinant protein production →purified fusion protein.

Results
1.1 Design of Expression Plasmids

Using the pET-28a(+) backbone, we designed three expression plasmids: pET-28a(+)-CPC, pET-28a(+)-LinkN, and pET-28a(+)-CPC+LinkN, with full lengths of 5,827 bp, 5,805 bp, and 5,887 bp, respectively (Table 1.1.1 and Figure 1.1.1). All three constructs used the same expression framework, containing a T7 promoter, lac operator, and kanamycin (Kan) resistance gene. From the N-terminus to the C-terminus, each target fusion protein contained a 6×His tag, SUMO fusion tag, TEV cleavage site, linker, CPC and/or Link-N sequence, AviTag, and DogTag. In the CPC+LinkN construct, CPC and Link-N were connected by a linker.

The three constructs differed only in their inserted sequences (Table 1.1.1): the CPC construct contained the CPC sequence; the Link-N construct contained Link-N and served as a CPC-free control; and the CPC+LinkN construct contained both CPC and Link-N, allowing us to assess whether Link-N fusion affected CPC-mediated GAG interactions.

1.2 Expression of CPC Recombinant Proteins and Optimization of Induction Conditions

The synthesized plasmids were transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) for protein expression. Colonies were obtained on Kan-containing plates for the transformed constructs (Figure 1.2.1), whereas no colonies grew on the control (CK) plate without plasmid transformation.

We then performed small-scale induction screening of the CPC expression system in E. coli BL21(DE3). The initial construct contained a repetitive CPC sequence designed in-house. We compared different IPTG concentrations, induction temperatures, and induction durations. After colony PCR validation, transformants were induced with 0.1–1.0 mM IPTG at 16 °C for 16 h or at 30 °C for 6 h. Additional conditions included 37 °C for 4 h and induction at 30 °C for 9 h or 16 h. Repeated SDS-PAGE analyses of the supernatant and pellet fractions revealed no clear induced bands at the expected positions; target bands were weak or diffuse, and background bands were also present in some uninduced samples. Consistent with these observations, His-tag affinity purification of both small- and large-scale cultures failed to enrich a clearly identifiable target protein: proteins were visible in the lysate and flow-through, but the eluate contained no band or only a very weak one (see Notebook). Thus, expanding the range of induction conditions alone did not resolve the expression bottleneck.

We therefore redesigned the CPC coding sequence using the literature-reported CPC+14A sequence, RRRR(AARRR)₃R, and performed codon optimization for E. coli while reducing sequence repetitiveness at the DNA level. The redesigned expression system yielded detectable CPC-containing recombinant proteins: SDS-PAGE showed identifiable target bands (Figure 1.2.2A), although some basal expression remained. The final induction condition was 30 °C with 0.5 mM IPTG for 16 h. SDS-PAGE after affinity purification showed enrichment of the target protein in the eluate (Figure 1.2.2B). Western blotting detected Link-N, CPC, and CPC–Link-N at the expected molecular-weight positions (Figure 1.2.2C), confirming successful expression of the target proteins. A weaker band was also visible in the uninduced control, indicating a degree of leaky expression.

1.3 His-Tag Affinity Purification and Concentration

Compare the lysate, flow-through, wash, and elution fractions of CPC, Link-N, and CPC–Link-N by SDS-PAGE (Figure 1.3.1). The target band was strongest in the Link-N eluate and weaker in the CPC-containing constructs, indicating substantial differences in the final recovery among constructs.

After His-tag affinity elution, the samples were concentrated and buffer-exchanged using 0.5-mL centrifugal ultrafiltration units with a 5-kDa molecular-weight cutoff. Protein concentrations were then measured by the BCA assay (standard curve R² = 0.9977; Figure 1.3.2a). The concentration of SUMO–Link-N was 17.51 mg/mL, whereas those of SUMO–CPC and SUMO–CPC–Link-N were only 0.43 mg/mL and 0.26 mg/mL, respectively (Figures 1.3.2b and 1.3.2c). The concentrations of the CPC-containing constructs were more than tenfold lower than that of the Link-N construct, suggesting that introduction of the CPC sequence substantially reduced recombinant-protein expression or recovery.

Experiment

Protein Concentration and SUMO Removal

After affinity purification, the recombinant protein was subjected to centrifugal ultrafiltration. This step was used to increase the protein concentration while simultaneously performing buffer exchange, thereby transferring the protein into conditions suitable for subsequent enzymatic cleavage.

The fusion protein was then treated with ULP1 to remove the SUMO domain. This step was performed because the downstream functional experiments focused on the actual CPC-containing functional construct rather than the complete expression fusion protein. At the same time, the AviTag was retained, allowing the processed protein to undergo BirA-mediated biotinylation and subsequent immobilization on streptavidin magnetic beads.

After SUMO cleavage, the sample was further analyzed to confirm tag removal and was subjected to another round of ultrafiltration to complete protein concentration and buffer exchange.After ULP1 cleavage, the final functional protein is AviTag-TEVsite-linker-DogTag-CPC.

Results
1.4 SUMO-Tag Removal and Reverse Purification

Cleavage products were clearly visible by SDS-PAGE (Figure 1.4.1a), indicating that SUMO removal occurred; however, cleavage was incomplete, and some uncleaved protein remained. BCA quantification yielded concentrations of 0.30 mg/mL for Link-N, 0.21 mg/mL for CPC, and 0.19 mg/mL for CPC–Link-N (Figures 1.4.1b–d).

In a separate BCA measurement, protein concentrations after reverse affinity purification, ultrafiltration, concentration, and buffer exchange were 1.42 mg/mL for Link-N, 0.14 mg/mL for CPC, and 0.69 mg/mL for CPC–Link-N (Figure 1.4.2). This workflow yielded further-processed proteins but introduced additional handling steps and was accompanied by some protein loss.

2. Validation of Ligation Activity and GAG-Binding Capability

After obtaining purified proteins, we first validated DogTag-mediated ligation activity. We then evaluated interactions between CPC-containing recombinant proteins and sulfated GAGs using a chondroitin sulfate A (CS-A) agarose electrophoretic mobility assay and an AviTag-based bead-immobilization assay with DMMB detection.

Experiment

Conjugation Activity Validation

Because the target CPC peptide is relatively small and therefore difficult to detect directly by electrophoresis, we introduced a GFP-SnoopTag reporter protein to examine whether the recovered CPC peptide retained DogTag-mediated conjugation activity. The CPC peptide and control peptide were subjected to conjugation reactions in parallel, with corresponding reactions lacking SnoopLigase included as controls.

After addition of the ligase, higher-molecular-weight bands corresponding to the conjugation products were observed, supporting the retention of DogTag-mediated conjugation activity by the CPC peptide. This model reaction also provided a readily detectable basis for validating the site-specific conjugation of CPC to the SELP scaffold in subsequent experiments. The assay validates the protein conjugation step and does not directly demonstrate successful anchoring of CPC within the SELP hydrogel.

Results
2.1 Validation of DogTag-Mediated Ligation Activity

After SnoopLigase2 was added, higher-molecular-weight bands consistent with SnoopTag2-GFP ligation products were observed at 55–70 kDa in lanes 1, 3, and 5 (red box in Figure 2.1.1). These bands disappeared or were markedly weaker in the corresponding ligase-free controls (lanes 2, 4, and 6). A ligation-product band was also observed at approximately 55 kDa in lane 7 (SUMO–DogTag control). These results support the conclusion that the recovered constructs retained DogTag-mediated ligation activity and could undergo specific ligation with SnoopTag2-GFP.

Experiment

CS-A Electrophoretic Mobility Analysis

We first examined whether the recombinant protein could interact with CS-A. CS-A is an important sulfated GAG in the cartilage extracellular matrix, while CPC is enriched in positively charged amino acids. We therefore expected that interaction between CPC and negatively charged CS-A would alter the migration behavior of CS-A in the electrophoresis system.

Before conducting the protein–GAG experiments, CS-A was first analyzed independently to confirm that a detectable GAG signal could be obtained under the established electrophoresis and staining conditions. The migration of CS-A was then compared under different protein conditions, with particular attention to whether increasing protein levels caused reduced migration distance, broader bands, or increased retention near the loading wells. This provided a direct molecular-level evaluation of the interaction between the recombinant protein and sulfated GAGs.

This experiment was primarily used as a binding screen. Because CS-A is a heterogeneous and polydisperse polymer, changes in electrophoretic mobility are suitable for determining whether an interaction occurs and assessing its relative changes.

This experiment therefore primarily addressed the first key question of the GAG-retention module:

Can the engineered CPC-containing recombinant protein still directly interact with sulfated GAGs at the molecular level?

Results
2.2 Establishment and Optimization of the CS-A Agarose Electrophoretic Mobility Assay

To directly assess interactions between CPC-containing recombinant proteins and sulfated GAGs, we first established a CS-A agarose electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA). CS-A alone and CS-A mixed with 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, or 10 µM SUMO– CPC, SUMO–CPC–Link-N, or SUMO–Link-N were analyzed by agarose gel electrophoresis (16 lanes in total), followed by toluidine blue staining. The initial electrophoresis duration was approximately 50 min, with bromophenol blue as the tracking dye. CS-A migrated substantially faster than bromophenol blue and had migrated too far by the end of the 50-min run for reliable comparison. Although CS-A was clearly visible, none of the proteins—including the CPC-free SUMO–Link-N control—caused an obvious change in migration distance, band width, or retention near the loading wells (see Notebook). These results indicated that the initial electrophoresis duration was unsuitable for the current CS-A detection system.

To rule out problems with the detection system itself, we analyzed CS-A alone at different loading amounts (1, 2, 5, and 10 µg). The CS-A-only controls produced clear, detectable GAG bands, and band intensity increased with loading amount (Figure 2.2.1), demonstrating that the current agarose electrophoresis and toluidine blue staining system could detect CS-A. The electrophoresis duration was therefore shortened to approximately 30–40 min.

After the electrophoresis duration was optimized, CS-A consistently appeared in a more suitable region of the gel for analysis. However, when different concentrations of CPC-containing fusion proteins were mixed with CS-A and analyzed again, no clear concentration-dependent mobility shift was observed. In other words, the system reliably detected CS-A, but adding the proteins did not produce a sufficiently clear migration change. Thus, the CS-A detection system was successfully established and optimized, but no clear positive CPC–CS-A readout was obtained through a mobility shift. This result does not directly demonstrate that CPC lacks GAG-binding activity, because migration may also be affected by molecular size, charge, conformation, and the state of the protein samples.

Experiment

AviTag-Mediated GAG Capture Assay

To complement the electrophoretic mobility assay, we established a second functional validation approach based on protein immobilization and GAG quantification.

Following ULP1 treatment, the recombinant protein retained the AviTag and was therefore first subjected to site-specific biotinylation using BirA. After biotinylation, free biotin was removed by desalting, and the protein concentration was re-measured by BCA. Biotinylation efficiency was verified by streptavidin gel shift or streptavidin-HRP Western blotting.The protein was then immobilized on streptavidin magnetic beads through the biotin–streptavidin interaction, thereby establishing an immobilized protein–GAG interaction system.

The immobilized protein was subsequently incubated with CS-A. After magnetic separation, the supernatant was collected and the remaining soluble CS-A was quantified using the DMMB assay.

Unlike the electrophoretic mobility assay, this experiment focused on whether immobilized protein could reduce the amount of CS-A remaining in solution. Naked magnetic bead controls and input controls were included to distinguish protein-dependent GAG capture from nonspecific adsorption by the magnetic beads and to determine the total amount of GAG at the beginning of the reaction.

Therefore, the primary readout of this experiment was the relative capture efficiency of CS-A by the immobilized protein.

From Molecular Binding to the GAG-Retention Design

The two experimental approaches validated the same molecular basis from different perspectives.

The CS-A electrophoretic mobility assay examined whether the CPC-containing protein altered the migration behavior of CS-A, whereas the streptavidin magnetic bead–DMMB assay further examined whether the immobilized protein could capture CS-A from solution.

Together, the two assays established a stepwise validation chain:

Plasmid construction →recombinant CPC protein production → purification and SUMO removal →protein–GAG interaction →GAG capture.

Results
2.3 CS-A Capture Assay Using an AviTag-Based Immobilization System
2.3.1 Site-Specific Biotinylation of AviTag

Biotinylation was assessed by SDS-PAGE, using non-biotinylated protein as the control (Figure 2.3.1.1). After incubation of non-biotinylated Link-N with SA, a free Link-N band was visible at approximately 15 kDa (red arrow). In contrast, this band disappeared or was markedly weaker when biotinylated Link-N, CPC, or CPC–Link-N was incubated with SA, while higher-molecular-weight bands associated with SA-containing complexes appeared near 70 kDa (red box). These observations suggest successful biotinylation and indicate that the resulting proteins could bind to streptavidin magnetic beads, establishing a basis for the subsequent protein–GAG interaction assay.

2.3.2 Bead Immobilization and DMMB-Based Detection of CS-A Capture

The experimental groups included bare beads (CK), the CPC-free Link-N protein control (L), CPC-containing protein (C), and CPC–Link-N (L+C). An Input CS-A sample without beads was also included to assess the initial substrate amount. These conditions were intended to examine background adsorption, the contribution of the protein components, and the starting substrate level, respectively. The assay response was calculated as the recorded OD525−OD600, and concentrations were derived using a common CS-A standard curve (y = 0.01309x + 0.04845, R² = 0.8888), followed by correction for the fourfold dilution. The original group labels CK, L, C, and L+C were retained. A decrease relative to CK is not, by itself, equivalent to capture efficiency corrected for bare-bead background.

The estimated CS-A concentrations in the supernatants, summarized across three replicate measurements, are shown in Figure 2.3.2.1a. In all three corresponding readings, the values for C and L+C were lower than CK, whereas the L group did not show a consistent downward trend. This pattern was consistent with the expectation that CPC-containing treatments would reduce the amount of CS-A remaining in the supernatant.

2.3.3 Statistical Analysis of the Reduction in Supernatant CS-A Associated with CPC and CPC–Link-N

To avoid drawing mechanistic conclusions directly from visual observations, we specified statistical hypotheses and applied multiple-comparison correction. This analysis assessed whether the reduction in supernatant CS-A was supported by statistical evidence and defined the scope of the conclusions that could be drawn.

CPC was compared with CK, and CPC–Link-N was compared with CK. Because each of the three treatment measurements corresponded one-to-one with a CK measurement, paired t-tests were used. For CPC versus CK, the difference for the iiith pair was defined as:

When the two prespecified comparisons were tested together, the Holm method was used to correct for multiple comparisons. The raw p-values, ranked from smallest to largest, were p(1)=0.0053, p(2)=0.0314p_{(1)}=0.0053,\ p_{(2)}=0.0314p(1)​=0.0053, p(2)​=0.0314, with the number of comparisons m = 2. The adjusted p-values were calculated as:

p(1)′=(m−1+1)×0.0053=0.0106p'_{(1)}=(m-1+1)\times0.0053=0.0106p(1)′​=(m−1+1)×0.0053=0.0106p(2)′=max⁡(p(1)′,(m−2+1)×0.0314)=0.0314p'_{(2)}=\max\left(p'_{(1)},(m-2+1)\times0.0314\right)=0.0314p(2)′​=max(p(1)′​,(m−2+1)×0.0314)=0.0314

After adjustment, the p-value for CPC–Link-N versus CK was 0.0106, and that for CPC versus CK was 0.0314. At a significance level of α = 0.05, both adjusted p-values were below 0.05; therefore, the null hypotheses that the mean differences between each treatment and CK were zero could be rejected.

In summary, the amount of residual CS-A in the supernatant was lower after treatment with both CPC and CPC–Link-N than in CK. Under the current dataset and analysis method, the results support an association between immobilized CPC or CPC–Link-N and reduced supernatant CS-A, in a direction consistent with the expected CPC-mediated GAG capture. However, because all measurements came from a single experiment (n = 3), this analysis should be considered exploratory.

Relationship to the Final SELP System

The experiments described above represent the molecular validation of the GAG-retention module. Their purpose was to determine whether the engineered CPC-containing protein retained the GAG interaction expected from the design.

Therefore, the current protein-level experiments first validate the molecular basis of CPC–GAG interaction, whereas whether CPC immobilized within the SELP hydrogel can truly reduce GAG loss represents a further material-level validation that requires direct evaluation through GAG retention/loss experiments in the hydrogel.

Through this approach, we progressively advanced the experimental logic from the smallest functional unit to the final biomaterial system:

engineered plasmid →recombinant protein →protein processing → molecular GAG interaction →GAG capture →hydrogel-level GAG retention.
delivery:
Mitochondrial Therapeutic Module

As part of developing a mitochondrial carrier and delivery system, we produced an engineered responsive peptide, verified its protein ligation activity and MMP responsiveness, and completed structural characterization and cellular delivery validation of liposome–mitochondria complexes.

1 Responsive Protein Expression

1.1 Expression Plasmid and Control Design

To obtain fusion proteins for subsequent ligation and cleavage assays, we designed the responsive expression plasmid pET28a-MMP13sp (Figure 1.1.1) and the control expression plasmid pET28a-Control (Figure 1.1.2) using the pET-28a vector backbone. Both plasmids are 5691 bp in length and share the same expression framework, including a T7 promoter and a kanamycin resistance gene. From the N-terminus to the C-terminus, each target fusion protein contains a 6×His tag, a SUMO fusion tag, a TEV protease cleavage site, a cysteine (Cys) conjugation site, the responsive or control segment, and DogTag. GGGGS linkers flank the responsive or control segment.

The responsive construct contains the peptide sequence RRGPLGLSLGKR, designed for cleavage by MMP-13, whereas the control construct contains the scrambled sequence RKGLSLGLPGRR in its place. Both sequences consist of 12 amino acids and have identical lengths and amino acid compositions, differing only in residue order. All other plasmid sequences remain identical. This control design enables comparison of cleavage behavior under identical treatment conditions and assessment of the contribution of the responsive sequence to proteolytic cleavage.

Both constructs retain the 6×His tag and TEV protease cleavage site for subsequent purification and tag removal, as well as the Cys site and DogTag for carrier conjugation and protein ligation. This shared design provides a basis for parallel expression and validation of ligation activity and MMP responsiveness.

1.2 Plasmid Transformation and Antibiotic Selection
Experiment

The two expression plasmids were separately transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3), and the transformed cells were plated onto LB agar supplemented with kanamycin for antibiotic selection.

Results

Following incubation, multiple discrete colonies were observed on the experimental plates, whereas no visible colony growth was detected on the uninoculated negative-control plate (Figure 1.2.1), supporting the recovery of putative transformants. Individual colonies were subsequently picked and expanded in culture for induction of fusion protein expression.

1.3 Fusion Protein Expression and Purification
Experiment

To identify suitable induction conditions, we compared protein expression at different IPTG concentrations. Preliminary screening showed relatively prominent target protein bands at 0.25 and 0.5 mM IPTG. Therefore, both conditions were selected for larger-scale expression.To address weak bands and insufficient separation in the initial electrophoretic analyses, we used Western blotting to assist target protein detection and further adjusted the expression and electrophoresis conditions.

Results

The experimental and control fusion proteins were subsequently purified separately by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography. Lysate, flow-through, wash, and elution fractions were collected for SDS-PAGE analysis. For both groups induced with 0.25 mM IPTG, bands in the 15–25 kDa range were enriched in the elution fractions (Figure 1.3.1), consistent with the expected molecular weight range of the target fusion proteins. These results support the expression and enrichment of both responsive and control fusion proteins.

The purified samples were dialyzed before use in subsequent experiments. One batch of the responsive peptide fusion protein had a measured concentration of 0.43 mg/mL, while the control protein sample had a measured concentration of 0.52 mg/mL. These preparations provided material for subsequent tag removal, protein ligation, and cleavage assays.

1.4 TEV Protease Cleavage and Functional Peptide Release
Experiment

To remove the SUMO tag from the responsive fusion protein and release the responsive peptide for subsequent ligation and functional assays, we incubated the purified fusion protein with TEV protease at 30 °C. Samples were collected after 1, 2, and 4 h of incubation, and a control without TEV protease was included. Cleavage was assessed by SDS-PAGE.

Results

Bands corresponding to the released SUMO tag were observed at all three time points in the TEV-treated samples, with an apparent molecular weight between 15 and 25 kDa (Figure 1.4.1). Their migration differed from that of the uncleaved fusion protein, supporting successful TEV-mediated removal of the SUMO tag. The bands indicated by yellow arrows correspond to the added TEV protease, with a molecular weight of approximately 27 kDa. These results provided a basis for subsequent isolation of the responsive peptide and protein ligation experiments.

Experiment

To evaluate the ligation activity of the functional peptide, we mixed the DogTag-containing peptide with the GFP-SnoopTag reporter protein and SnoopLigase, incubated the mixture at room temperature for 1 h, and analyzed the reaction products by SDS-PAGE. SnoopLigase-mediated ligation of SUMO-DogTag to GFP-SnoopTag served as the positive control, while a reaction without SnoopLigase served as the negative control.

Results

Compared with the negative control, the peptide reaction produced an additional higher-molecular-weight band above the main GFP-SnoopTag band (Figure 1.4.2). This mobility shift was consistent with the formation of a peptide–GFP-SnoopTag conjugate. The bands indicated by yellow arrows correspond to SnoopLigase, with an apparent molecular weight between 10 and 15 kDa. These results support the presence of a peptide retaining DogTag-mediated ligation activity in the recovered sample. The resulting conjugate also provided a reporter substrate detectable by electrophoresis for subsequent studies of MMP responsiveness.

Given the low concentration of the recovered peptide, we subsequently concentrated the samples by lyophilization to meet the sample requirements for downstream ligation and cleavage assays.

2 Construction and Characterization of the Liposomal Delivery System

2.1 Mitochondrial Isolation and Fraction Characterization
Experiment

To prepare liposome–mitochondria complexes, we first isolated mitochondrial samples and examined the mitochondrial marker proteins COX IV, an inner membrane protein, and TOMM20, an outer membrane protein.

Results

Western blot analysis detected both proteins in the isolated pellet fraction, supporting the presence of mitochondrial components in the preparation (Figure 2.1.1). These samples provided material for subsequent carrier assembly.

2.2 Preparation of Functionalized Liposomes
Experiment

To construct a carrier for mitochondrial delivery that could also be coupled to the engineered linker peptide, we prepared functionalized liposomes using DOPE, DOTAP, and DSPE-PEG-Mal. DSPE-PEG-Mal was incorporated to provide maleimide groups for subsequent conjugation with the Cys thiol group in the linker peptide.

Results

The resulting liposome suspension had a milky-white appearance (Figure 2.2.1). We then co-incubated the liposomes with isolated mitochondria to form liposome–mitochondria complexes. Fluorescence imaging and transmission electron microscopy were used to further evaluate the spatial association between the components and the encapsulation morphology.

2.3 Characterization of the Complexes
2.3.1 Confocal Fluorescence Characterization
Experiment

To examine the spatial distribution of liposomes and mitochondria, we labeled them with DiD and MitoTracker Green, respectively. The assembled complexes were then examined by confocal fluorescence microscopy, acquiring green and red fluorescence images alongside bright-field images.

Results

MitoTracker Green-labeled mitochondria exhibited green fluorescence, while DiD-labeled liposomes exhibited red fluorescence. The two signals overlapped at multiple locations, producing yellow–orange regions in the merged image (Figure 2.3.1). These observations support a spatial association between liposomes and mitochondria. Transmission electron microscopy was subsequently used to evaluate whether the mitochondria were encapsulated by liposomes.

2.3.2 Structural Characterization by Transmission Electron Microscopy
Experiment

To further evaluate the encapsulation structure of liposome–mitochondria complexes, we used transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to examine functionalized liposomes, free mitochondria, and assembled complexes, comparing their morphological and structural features (Figure 2.3.2).

Results

Vesicle-like structures and membrane outlines were observed in the liposome samples (Figure 2.3.2A). In the liposome–mitochondria complexes, peripheral membrane-like structures surrounded internal components (Figure 2.3.2C). This morphology was consistent with the expected configuration of mitochondria encapsulated by liposomes, providing morphological support for encapsulation. Together with the overlap of the two fluorescence signals observed by confocal microscopy, these findings support the formation of liposome–mitochondria complexes.

2.4 Preliminary Evaluation of Linker Peptide–Liposome Conjugation
Experiment

To integrate the liposomal carrier into the protein ligation system, we attempted to conjugate the linker peptide to the liposome surface through the reaction between the Cys thiol group and surface maleimide groups. Following the reaction, ultrafiltration was used to separate unbound peptide, and protein quantification was performed to assess conjugation.

Results

During this evaluation, ultrafiltration resulted in inconsistent sample recovery and sample loss, while the liposome formulation interfered with colorimetric protein assays. These limitations prevented the current methods from distinguishing the contributions of covalent conjugation, nonspecific adsorption, and losses during separation to the measured results. Therefore, a reduction in free peptide after separation alone cannot establish successful conjugation, and conjugation efficiency cannot yet be reliably determined.

Further work is needed to optimize the separation and quantification methods and incorporate sample recovery measurements and liposomes lacking maleimide groups as controls. These steps are intended to establish a reliable workflow for validating conjugation and support integration of the delivery carrier with the SELP scaffold.

3 Functional Validation

3.1 Validation of SnoopLigase-Mediated Ligation of the Linker Peptide
Experiment

To evaluate the ligation activity of the DogTag module within the linker peptide, we separately mixed the responsive protein (MMP13-DogTag) and the scrambled control protein (Control-DogTag) with the GFP-SnoopTag reporter protein. Reactions with and without SnoopLigase were included, and ligation product formation was analyzed by SDS-PAGE.

Results

A higher-molecular-weight band near 55 kDa was observed in both the responsive and control reactions containing SnoopLigase (Figure 3.1.1), whereas no distinct band at the same position was observed in the corresponding reactions without the enzyme. This mobility shift was consistent with the expected increase in molecular weight following ligation of each protein to GFP-SnoopTag, supporting the formation of SnoopLigase-mediated ligation products.

These results support the retention of DogTag-mediated ligation activity in both the responsive and scrambled control proteins and provide an experimental basis for subsequent comparison of the MMP-13 cleavage responses of the two reporter substrates.

3.2 Validation of MMP-13-Mediated Cleavage of the Responsive Linker Peptide
Experiment

To evaluate the MMP-13 responsiveness of the linker peptide, we separately ligated the responsive peptide (Pep) and the scrambled control peptide (Control) to GFP-SnoopTag, generating reporter substrates detectable by electrophoresis. The conjugates were subsequently treated with MMP-13, and samples were collected at 0, 2, 4, 6, and 24 h for SDS-PAGE analysis of changes in the band patterns.

Results

Differences in band patterns between the Pep and Control groups were evident at 2 h. The Control group retained a slower-migrating band near 35 kDa, corresponding to the uncleaved GFP–peptide conjugate (Figure 3.2.1), whereas the corresponding higher-molecular-weight band in the Pep group was weaker or not clearly detectable. This pattern was consistent with cleavage of the responsive peptide conjugate, suggesting susceptibility to MMP-13 cleavage. Further comparisons with substrate samples collected before enzyme addition and matched controls without MMP-13 are needed to confirm whether the observed differences arise from enzymatic cleavage rather than differences in the initial composition of the ligation products.

3.3 Evaluation of Cellular Delivery by Liposome–Mitochondria Complexes
Experiment

To evaluate the cellular delivery capability of liposome–mitochondria complexes, we first labeled isolated mitochondria with MitoTracker Green and then co-incubated the labeled mitochondria with liposomes to form the complexes. The complexes were subsequently added to recipient cell cultures. Hoechst 33342 nuclear staining, together with bright-field and fluorescence imaging, was used to examine the distribution of labeled mitochondria within the cells.

Results

Green fluorescence was observed in cells treated with the complexes. In the merged images, the green signals were distributed within the cell outlines and in perinuclear regions (Figure 3.3.1A), whereas no distinct corresponding green fluorescence was observed in the control group (Figure 3.3.1B). These findings suggest that exogenous mitochondria in the complexes can enter recipient cells, providing preliminary imaging evidence supporting cellular delivery by liposome–mitochondria complexes.

3.4 Biosafety Evaluation
Experiment

To preliminarily assess the in vitro cytocompatibility of the functional peptide, we used the CCK-8 assay to measure relative cell viability following peptide treatment. The experiment included control, blank, and peptide-treated groups (Figure 3.4.1A). Cell viability was evaluated after treatment with 5 or 10 μM peptide for 24, 48, and 72 h.

Results

At 24 h, relative cell viability was approximately 70% and 55% in the 5 and 10 μM groups, respectively. At 48 h, viability increased to approximately 85%–90% in both groups and remained within approximately 85%–95% at 72 h (Figure 3.4.1B). These results indicate that cells treated with peptide concentration exhibited relatively high viability at the later time points.

The lower cell viability at 24 h may have been related to the initial condition of the cells. However, the available data cannot clearly distinguish the influence of initial cell condition from the effects of peptide treatment. This experiment provides preliminary data on the cytocompatibility of the functional peptide. Further validation through repeated experiments with standardized initial cell conditions is needed to clarify the causes of the early changes in viability and identify suitable treatment conditions.
